claim: Spatial frequency (SF) constitutes a pivotal component of visual stimuli encoding in the primate visual system, encompassing the number of grating cycles within a specific visual angle.
source: Spatial frequency (SF) constitutes a pivotal component of visual stimuli encoding in the primate visual system, encompassing the number of grating cycles within a specific visual angle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about spatial frequency in visual neuroscience.

claim: Higher SF (HSF) corresponds to intricate details, while lower SF (LSF) captures broader information.
source: Higher SF (HSF) corresponds to intricate details, while lower SF (LSF) captures broader information.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between spatial frequency and visual detail.

claim: Previous psychophysical studies have compellingly demonstrated the profound influence of SF manipulation on object recognition and categorization processes.
source: Previous psychophysical studies have compellingly demonstrated the profound influence of SF manipulation on object recognition and categorization processes (Joubert et al., 2007; Schyns and Oliva, 1994; Ashtiani et al., 2017; Caplette et al., 2014; Cheung and Bar, 2014; Craddock et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: HSF and LSF are significant for categorical/coordinate processing and in object recognition and decision-making.
source: Jahfari et al., 2013 and Saneyoshi and Michimata, 2015 have highlighted the significance of HSF and LSF for categorical/coordinate processing and in object recognition and decision-making, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Coarse-to-fine presentation of SF content leads to faster categorizations.
source: The sequence in which SF content is presented also affects the categorization performance, with coarse-to-fine presentation leading to faster categorizations (Kauffmann et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Middle and higher SFs are more critical for face recognition.
source: Considering face as a particular object, several studies showed that middle and higher SFs are more critical for face recognition (Cheung et al., 2008; Costen et al., 1996; Fiorentini et al., 1983; Hayes et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The coarse-to-fine perception theory states that LSF or global contents are processed faster than HSF or local contents.
source: Another vital theory suggested by psychophysical studies is the coarse-to-fine perception of visual stimuli, which states that LSF or global contents are processed faster than HSF or local contents (Gao and Bentin, 2011; Kauffmann et al., 2015; Rokszin et al., 2016; Rotshtein et al., 2010; Schyns and Oliva, 1994; Yardley et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Understanding of SF representation within primate visual systems, particularly in higher visual areas like the inferior temporal (IT) cortex, remains constrained due to limited research.
source: Despite the extensive reliance on psychophysical studies to examine the influence of SF on categorization tasks, our understanding of SF representation within primate visual systems, particularly in higher visual areas like the inferior temporal (IT) cortex, remains constrained due to the limited research in this specific domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of existing literature.

claim: Bar, 2003 proposed a top–down mechanism driven by the rapid processing of LSF content, facilitating object recognition.
source: Their research proposes a top–down mechanism driven by the rapid processing of LSF content, facilitating object recognition (Bar, 2003; Fenske et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Distinct brain regions are engaged in processing various SF contents.
source: The exploration of SF representation has revealed the engagement of distinct brain regions in processing various SF contents (Bastin et al., 2013; Bermudez et al., 2009; Chaumon et al., 2014; Cheung and Bar, 2014; Fintzi and Mahon, 2014; Gaska et al., 1988; Iidaka et al., 2004; Oram and Perrett, 1994; Peyrin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex accesses global (LSF) and local (identity; HSF) information in the right and left hemispheres, respectively.
source: More specifically, the orbitofrontal cortex has been identified as accessing global (LSF) and local (identity; HSF) information in the right and left hemispheres, respectively (Fintzi and Mahon, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The V3A area exhibits low-pass tuning curves.
source: The V3A area exhibits low-pass tuning curves (Gaska et al., 1988), while HSF processing activates the left fusiform gyrus (Iidaka et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: HSF processing activates the left fusiform gyrus.
source: The V3A area exhibits low-pass tuning curves (Gaska et al., 1988), while HSF processing activates the left fusiform gyrus (Iidaka et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Neural responses in the IT cortex demonstrate correlations with the SF components of complex stimuli.
source: Neural responses in the IT cortex, which play a pivotal role in object recognition and face perception, demonstrate correlations with the SF components of complex stimuli (Bermudez et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

source: SF decoding is observed in both population- and single-level representations.

claim: SF coding exhibits a coarse-to-fine pattern, emphasizing faster processing of lower frequencies.
